meta.reproducibility: All probabilities come from the vetted Elo->Poisson->Monte-Carlo model in code/simulate.py (run from DATA_DIR; deterministic at seed 20260618, N=100000). simulate.py was re-run and reproduced the published forecast_outputs/ CSVs exactly. Derived journalism findings are computed in code/story_findings.py, which reads those published CSVs.

dataset.what_one_row_represents: One of the 48 qualified teams, with its Elo, FIFA rank, squad market value and simulated probabilities of advancing through each round to the title.
dataset.time_range: Forecast as of 2026-06-24 (46 of 72 group games played); Elo fit on internationals 1872-06 to 2026-06-23.
dataset.geographic_scope: Global — 48 national teams across 6 confederations; tournament hosted by USA/Canada/Mexico.

ana_01.label: Champion odds — Argentina 30.3% leads a steep ladder
ana_01.content: As of the 2026-06-24 snapshot, the model gives Argentina the best chance of lifting the trophy at 30.3%, ahead of Spain (22.1%), France (13.7%), England (8.4%), Colombia (5.7%) and Portugal (3.6%). The distribution is steep and top-heavy: the top two account for more than half of all title probability, and only 13 of the 48 teams have even a 1% chance. These are championship probabilities — the share of 100,000 simulated tournaments each team wins — and they sum to 1.000 across the field. Argentina leads not because it is guaranteed anything, but because across every plausible bracket it survives more often than anyone else.

ana_02.label: Where the model fights the FIFA ranking
ana_02.content: A results-trained Elo model re-orders the official FIFA ladder, and among the 13 real contenders the disagreements are sharp. The model's biggest upgrade is Norway, ranked 31st by FIFA but lifted to the 10th-best title chance (1.8%); next is Colombia, FIFA's 13th but the model's 5th pick at 5.7%, then Japan (FIFA 18th up to 12th) and Germany (10th up to 8th). In the other direction the model fades market darlings: Morocco drops from FIFA 7th to 11th, Portugal from 5th to 6th. At the very top the two systems agree — Argentina is first on both, England fourth on both. Where they part ways is where a reader has the most room to argue.

ana_03.label: Money vs. merit — Colombia is five times cheaper than France
ana_03.content: Squad market value and simulated success only loosely track each other. France carries the costliest squad in the tournament at €1.52bn and the model gives it a 45.2% chance of reaching the semi-finals — €34m of squad value per percentage point of that chance. Colombia's squad costs €302m, roughly a fifth of France's, yet the model still gives it a 24.1% semi-final chance, at just €13m per point — more than twice as efficient. The clearest bargains are Argentina (€12m per semi-final point) and Colombia; the most expensive by this measure are Portugal (€51m per point) and Germany (€56m). The market pays for names; the model counts results.

ana_04.label: The bracket is a coin-flip for three teams
ana_04.content: Because only the top two of each group advance automatically and the eight best third-placed teams fill the rest of the new Round of 32, qualification splits the field into two worlds. Seventeen teams are already all but through (reach-R32 probability of 99% or more): Argentina, Mexico, Switzerland, Canada and others. But three teams sit on a true knife edge, with a reach-R32 probability between 40% and 60% — Senegal (55.5%), Bosnia & Herzegovina (48.0%) and DR Congo (41.4%) — for whom a single result swings the whole tournament. For those three, the model isn't predicting so much as describing a coin still in the air.

ana_05.label: Two confederations own 94% of the title chance
ana_05.content: The title race is geographically narrow. European (UEFA) teams hold a combined 55.2% of all championship probability and South American (CONMEBOL) teams another 39.7% — together 94.9% of the entire field's title chance. The remaining four confederations split the last 5.1% between them: North/Central America (CONCACAF) 1.8%, Asia (AFC) 1.6%, Africa (CAF) 1.6%, and Oceania (OFC) effectively 0%. Every one of the model's top six is European or South American. The 48-team field is the broadest ever, but the favourites still come from the same two continents that have won every men's World Cup.

ana_06.label: Why believe it — beats a naive baseline on 8,000 games, close on these 46
ana_06.content: The forecast earns trust by being checked, and the check is reported honestly. On a large out-of-sample test of 8,000 historical internationals the model clearly beats a naive baseline (which just predicts the home/draw/away base rates): log-loss 0.899 versus 1.062 — about 15% lower error — and 58.9% result accuracy versus 48.3%. That is the reliable read. On the 46 games of THIS World Cup already played, the model and the naive baseline are close (log-loss 0.943 vs 1.061; accuracy 58.7% vs 54.3%). A 46-game sample is small and upset-prone, so it is supporting evidence, not the verdict. The honest position: the method is sound on the long run, and the early tournament has, if anything, broken the model's way.

ana_07.label: Who you'd play is itself a distribution — 495 of them
ana_07.content: Even for a team that is certain to advance, the model cannot name its Round-of-32 opponent yet, because the pairings depend on which eight of the twelve third-placed teams qualify. FIFA's Annex C tabulates all C(12,8) = 495 of those combinations, and the simulation integrates over every one. Argentina, for example, reaches the Round of 32 in essentially 100% of simulations, but the team it meets there is spread across many possible opponents — a distribution, not a fixture. This is the structural reason a mid-tournament forecast for the first 48-team World Cup has to be probabilistic about the bracket itself, not just the results.

calculation.output:
Because R32 pairings depend on which 8 of 12 thirds qualify, 'who you'd meet' is a

  Argentina reaches R32 with p=100.0% but its
  specific opponent is not fixed until the group stage ends - the model averages over all 495.
  best-thirds table rows = 495 (FIFA Annex C)

ana_histbase.label: Is 30.3% a lot? Only eight nations have ever won
ana_histbase.content: So the model says Argentina, at 30.3%, is the team to beat — and history is unkind to favourites. Only eight nations have ever won a men's World Cup, and just three of them — Brazil (5), Italy (4) and Germany (4) — hold 13 of the 22 titles (59%). Six repeat champions account for 20 of 22 (91%). Even home advantage has converted only about 27% of the time (six host winners in twenty-two). Read against a long-run favourite hit-rate of ~23%, Argentina's 30.3% sits about seven points above the bar: a slightly-stronger-than-usual favourite, not a lock.

ana_goals.label: The race for the Golden Boot — and goals that arrive late
ana_goals.content: With the group stage all but done, Lionel Messi leads the 2026 World Cup scoring chart on five goals — a hat-trick against Algeria and a brace against Austria, every one from open play — with Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappe a goal back on four. Across the 139 goals scored so far the busiest single window is just before half-time (31-45, 18.7%), but the more striking pattern is late: 25.9% of goals have come from the 76th minute on, and 10.8% in stoppage time alone. The tournament has leaned on open play (89.2% of goals) with penalties rarer than the long-run norm (4.3%) and own goals unusually common (6.5%).

ana_shootouts.label: Penalty shootouts are a coin flip — even for the favourite
ana_shootouts.content: The model's analytic shortcut for knockout ties is forgivable because penalties are close to a coin toss. Across 678 international shootouts (1967-2026) the higher pre-match-Elo team — the favourite by the same Elo used everywhere else — won just 53.7% (two-sided binomial p=0.06 vs 50%), even though those favourites averaged a 114-point Elo edge worth about a 66% win rate in normal play. Tighten to the most lopsided ties (Elo gap >=150) and the favourite still wins only 55.7%. The team shooting first wins 53.1% of the 256 shootouts with a recorded first kicker — and at the World Cup finals specifically, just 17 of 35 (48.6%).

caveats.content: Group ranking uses points, then goal difference, then goals for, then a random tiebreak; full head-to-head tiebreakers are not implemented (rarely decisive).
Knockout extra-time and penalties are modelled by an Elo win-expectation term, not simulated minute-by-minute.
All World Cup matches are treated as neutral-venue; host advantage for the USA, Canada and Mexico is not modelled.
Goals are independent Poisson draws; no Dixon-Coles low-score correction and no red-card or injury effects.
Squad market value and FIFA rank are carried for context only; the forecast is driven by Elo. Monte-Carlo numbers carry sampling noise of roughly +/-0.3pp on champion odds at N=100,000.
